title: Track 7, Lesson 2: Growth investing - betting on the future instead of today's value
subtitle: Unlike value investing, growth investing accepts a high price today in exchange for rapid growth tomorrow.
whyItMatters: Many well-known technology shares (compounding hard for years) are nowhere near "cheap" by value standards. Understanding growth investing helps you judge when paying a high price is reasonable, and when it is just FOMO.
openingQuestion: A share has a P/E (price to earnings) far above its sector average. What does that always mean?
openingOptions: Not necessarily anything - exceptional growth can justify a high P/E
A high P/E means the company is making heavy losses and will soon be unable to continue operating as a business
The share is certainly overvalued against its real worth and investors should stay away from it entirely
The share is certainly a good opportunity to buy immediately, with no need for any further analysis at all
explanation: Growth investing accepts a high multiple today in exchange for the expectation of much larger profits within a few years. The point to grasp is that you are buying a forecast, so the risk is not that the business does badly but that it grows more slowly than the price already assumes. A business growing 20% a year can still lose half its value if the market had been expecting 35%.

diagram.label: The future P/E becomes reasonable - if the expectation holds

realWorldExample.description: Many technology companies hold a P/E far above the market average for years on end because profits keep compounding at 30-40% a year - growth investors accept the high price because they believe that trajectory continues.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk in growth investing?
options: Growth shares are taxed more heavily than other kinds of shares
Growth shares usually pay no cash dividend at all
If growth misses expectations, the price corrects sharply
Liquidity in growth shares is always extremely low
quiz.explanation: Because the price already reflects high growth expectations, a company growing more slowly than forecast (while still growing) can see its price fall sharply - the risk that distinguishes growth shares from value shares.

quiz.question: Company A has a P/E of 15 (low) and profit growth of 5% a year. Company B has a P/E of 50 (high) and profit growth of 35% a year. After 5 years, assuming growth holds, whose 'actual' P/E (on year-5 profits) becomes more reasonable?
options: Company A - a P/E of 15 was already reasonable and needs no change
Company B - profits multiply ~4.5 times, pulling the P/E right down
Company B, but only if the share price stands still for 5 years
Both equally, because P/E does not change over time
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the logic of growth investing: (1.35)^5 ≈ 4.48 times company B's original profit, pulling its forward P/E from 50 down to about 11 if growth arrives as forecast - below company A's current P/E of 15. The risk is that this 'if' is not always right.

quiz.question: On what reasoning does a growth investor accept a high P/E?
options: Believing profits grow fast enough to make the future P/E reasonable
Believing a high P/E is evidence that the business is well managed
Believing the market will push the P/E even higher in the near future
Believing companies on high P/Es pay larger dividends than others do
quiz.explanation: Paying a P/E of 40 for a company growing profits at 40% a year means the effective P/E is about 20 two years later. The whole argument rests on 'if' - if that growth actually happens.

quiz.question: What is the PEG ratio used for?
options: Measuring the dividend a growth company pays against its sector rivals
Comparing P/E with the growth rate to see whether the price matches expectations
Measuring the debt-to-equity ratio of businesses that are currently growing
Comparing the current share price with the highest price of the past fifty-two weeks
quiz.explanation: PEG is the P/E divided by the growth rate, and around 1 is generally considered reasonable. Its weakness is the denominator: it is a forecast, and the whole conclusion depends on the number you feed in.

quiz.question: Why is the line between value and growth investing increasingly blurred?
options: Because funds may now only register under exactly one of the two schools
Because the law merged these two schools into a single category years ago
Because an undervalued growth company is also a value share
Because growth shares now all trade on lower P/Es than value shares
quiz.explanation: Buffett said growth is part of the value calculation rather than an opposing school. The final question is always the same: is the price being paid below the value of the future cash flows?

quiz.question: What suggests a company's growth story is starting to wobble?
options: The share price moving sideways for months while the market rises slightly
The company beginning to publish full financial statements each quarter
The number of shares outstanding falling as the company buys back stock
Revenue growth slowing while the cost of acquiring a customer rises
quiz.explanation: This pair usually turns bad before profits do: it costs more to win each additional customer while revenue growth stalls. That is when a high multiple starts losing its support.

keyTakeaways: Growth investing: accept a high P/E today in exchange for fast profit growth tomorrow
A high P/E is not automatically 'expensive' if growth is fast enough and durable
The main risk: growth missing expectations → a sharp correction, because the price is no longer justified

practicePrompt.question: Company Z trades on a P/E of 45, far above its sector average of 18, but profits have grown steadily at 30% a year for the past 3 years. A friend says 'a P/E that high must be expensive, avoid it'. Is that right?
options: Not entirely - if 30% growth holds, the effective future P/E falls sharply
Completely right, because a P/E above the sector average always means without exception that a share is overpriced
Wrong, because a high P/E is always a good sign showing the company will certainly keep growing strongly in future
Irrelevant to analysing a share at all, because the P/E ratio has no meaning when comparing different companies
practicePrompt.explanation: A high P/E is not automatically 'expensive' if growth is fast enough and durable - but the risk is that if real growth misses expectations, the price can correct sharply because a high P/E is no longer justified.

summary.keyIdea: Growth investing: accept a high P/E today in exchange for fast profit growth tomorrow
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: A high P/E is not automatically 'expensive' if growth is fast enough and durable

application.title: Try the analysis
application.message: The lesson already carries a real example in FPT's P/E (~10.5 times, profit growth ~17% a year) - see the 'Real example' section above. Now find another growth share and apply the same analysis.
application.secondary: If the rate needed sounds unrealistic, that is a signal to be cautious.

sections.text: Where value investing hunts for a gap between price and present value, growth investing bets on a different story: this business will get large enough, fast enough, that today's high price turns out to be cheap when seen from a few years out.
A high P/E does not mean expensive

P/E (price/earnings) is the number of years of current profit needed to 'repay' the share price. A P/E of 15 means paying 15 dong for each dong of this year's profit. A growth investor will pay 30, 50 or more if they believe profits will rise fast enough that the forward P/E - measured on profits a few years out - returns to a reasonable level.
Example: when a P/E of 50 is cheaper than a P/E of 15

Compare company A (P/E 15, profit growth 5% a year) with company B (P/E 50, profit growth 35% a year). After 5 years, if growth arrives as expected, company B's profit is (1.35)^5 ≈ 4.48 times larger. B's P/E measured on year-5 profits falls from 50 to about 11 - below company A's current 15. That is the logic of growth investing: paying a high price today to buy a much cheaper one in the future, provided the growth materialises.
The word 'if' carries all the risk

The problem is that the price already reflects high growth expectations at the moment you buy. If the company grows 20% instead of 35% - still positive, still good growth - the market may treat that as a 'disappointment' and sell heavily, because a P/E of 50 is no longer justified. Growth shares therefore tend to swing harder than value shares on bad news, even when the business itself is not collapsing.

left.label: Value investing
left.text: Buying a proven business below its present value, with a wide margin of safety and less dependence on forecasting the future correctly.

right.label: Growth investing
right.text: Buying a business that is accelerating, at a price reflecting future expectations - large gains if right, sharp corrections if growth slows.

items: Check whether profit growth is durable, or just one exceptional year
Compare the current P/E with the forward P/E on realistic growth, not the most optimistic case
Accept larger swings - growth shares usually fall further when the market corrects
Don't concentrate the whole portfolio into a few 'hot' growth shares at once

sections.text: A real example: FPT's P/E and the growth question

items: FPT trades on a forward P/E of about 10.5 times, well below its 3-year average of 18.4 times
Profit after tax in 2025 rose 19.37% on 2024; the 2026 forecast adds about 13%, with a 2025-2028 CAGR of roughly 17% a year

The growth question: with a P/E of 10.5 and profit growth of ~17% a year, does that valuation reflect the growth rate, or is the market marking it down over a separate concern (here, the risk of AI displacing traditional IT services)?

sections.label: How to run this on another share
sections.text: Pick a growth share, look up its current P/E, and compare it with forecast profit growth (from a brokerage research note). A P/E divided by the growth rate (%) close to 1 is generally considered a reasonable valuation (the PEG ratio).
